messages.subject: secr 3.1.3
messages.body_plain:
A new version of secr is now on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=secr.

See http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/News.html for highlights. The new 'capped' detector type will be explained at length in a future vignette (tentatively secr-detectortypes.pdf).

A few seldom-used functions have new names in 3.1.3 (derived.mash becomes derivedMash, etc.). A bug in sim.capthist foiled attempts to simulate learned responses (since about April, now fixed).

Murray

> To: secr
> Subject: Re: Questions regarding secr.test, hazard-rate detection function and extracting variance estimates from a fitted model
>

> Taking this further...
>
> For session-specific estimates of finite population increase (lambda) I found a way to use a different coding of the 'session' factor. This requires a tweak to secr - now included in release 3.1.1 submitted to CRAN a few minutes ago and available in the meantime as Windows binary secr_3.1.1.zip <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.1.zip> or source secr_3.1.1.tar.gz <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.1.tar.gz>. The tweak allows users to specify the contrasts used in coding factor predictors (such as 'session').
>
> The idea is spelled out in the 'Trend across sessions' section of  secr-multisession.pdf <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-multisession.pdf>.
>
> Murray
>
>
> On Wednesday, November 29, 2017 at 8:49:55 AM UTC+13, Murray Efford wrote:
> >
> > > Firstly, are the results from the secr.test interpreted the same as the bootstrapped GOF test in program MARK? (e.g. the lower the value of P, the more you have to worry about lack of fit (page 5-22 in Program MARK –a gentle introduction-).
> >
> > I don't know MARK that well, but I expect the answer is Yes
> >
> > >
> > > Is it ever ok to use the hazard rate detection function? When I use AIC to compare models with differnt detection functions, the models with hazard rate or exponential detection functions always have the smallest AIC values. In most of the stuff I have read, using hazard rate is discouraged unless there is some kind of boundary. The population I am studying is on an island. Is it therefore ok to use the hazard rate detection function? I only ask because the density estimates are considerably different depending on which detection function is used.
> >
> > The main problem with the hazard-rate function, andalso  the reason it may fit better than say halfnormal, is its long tail, which accommodates occasional long movements. A long tail means that very distant animals have a chance to get caught and the population at risk of detection is enormous. On an island there will be a natural boundary rather than an arbitrary cutoff, so this is less of a worry. The exponential function serves nearly the same purpose but is better behaved in the tail. If the different detection functions result in very different estimates I would be careful - those long movements may be having far too much influence.
> > >
> > > Lastly, I would like to calculate population change (lambda= Dt+1/Dt) and the associated standard error (SE(lambdai) =  ).
> > >
> > >
> > >  Is there any way that I can extract the variance estimate for density from a fitted model so that I can calculate SE(lambdai)?
> > >
> > >
> >
> > I don't quite get the question. 'secr' reports SE for density. If you are interested in multiplicative population change between sessions then the beta coefficient D.Session of a model with D ~ Session (not capital S) is log(lambda) (assuming the default log link for density). So lambda-hat = exp(beta-hat) and SE(lambda-hat) = exp(beta-hat) * sqrt(exp(sebeta-hat^2)-1) (the standard delta approximation used in 'secr'). For the ovenbird example in 'secr'
> > beta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'beta']
> > sebeta <- coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', 'SE.beta']
> > exp(beta)
> > [1] 0.9381417
> > exp(beta) * sqrt(exp(sebeta^2)-1)
> > [1] 0.06589315
> > # 95% CI by backtransforming limits on log scale
> > exp(coef(ovenbird.model.D)['D.Session', c('lcl','ucl')])
> >                 lcl     ucl
> > D.Session 0.8176272 1.07642
> >
> > Murray
>

messages.subject: pooled detection from multiple years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,
I am trying to estimate the density of tiger. The study sites were two areas in the same national park, but both sites were far apart with no individuals move between two areas (no same captured animal found in both sites). No home range study available in this national park to understand how far the animals can move. First study site conducted on Dec 12-May 13, and second site conducted Nov 13 -Aug14. In total, I captured nine individuals from both areas, but the movement was observed only at first site (with a few recapture).
My question is Can I combine two data sets to estimate the density represent for this national park?

Best regards,
Dusit

messages.subject: Spatial covariate question
messages.body_plain:
Used hair snares for a black bear density estimate in Wyoming and secr has worked great except I have been having quite a bit of trouble with the addCovariates function.  I apologize if this is a rudimentary question but I haven't been able to figure out what I'm doing wrong.  I converted a raster layer of forest cover to a SpatialGridDataFrame which works but when I try to add it to the mask I created (a trap buffer) I get an error.

bbgrey <- read.capthist (captfile = 'secr_input3.txt',
                         trapfile = 'SnareSitesRelabel.txt',
                         fmt = "trapID", detector = "proximity", comment.char = "#", covnames = "sex")

#create buffer
maskWR10 <- make.mask (traps(bbgrey), type = "trapbuffer", buffer = 10000, nx = 64)

rusty <- raster("C:/Users/Rykinder/Desktop/Black Bear 2017/forest/majhalfexputm/w001w001.adf")
cropbox <- c(498694, 562893, 4680651, 4801089)
rusty2 <- crop(rusty, cropbox)
rusty3 <- as(rusty2, "SpatialGridDataFrame")
> maskWR101 <- addCovariates(maskWR10,rusty3,"VALUE")
Error in `[.data.frame`(df, , columns, drop = FALSE) :
  undefined columns selected

The photo below depicts the trap sites (blue dots), buffer (white), and a forest cover layer (purple and green). Do I need to clip the forest cover to be the same shape as the buffer or is there something else wrong. Please let me know if you need any other information and thanks for the help in advance.

Ryan

messages.subject: Re: pooled detection from multiple years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dusit
There is no technical reason why you cannot combine datasets and fit a model assuming the same detection parameters apply in both areas. I feel obliged to warn that with such small numbers you should not take _any_ capture-recapture estimate very seriously; the 8-month duration of the second sample will ring alarm bells for some people because of the potential for population turnover, but this is probably a minor issue compared to the small sample size.
Cheers
Murray

Why not D~spcov?

Note that fitting a fully sex-specific model (D~g, g0~g, sigma~g) is just a painfully slow way of getting two independent estimates, one for males and one for females. Could instead use something like
CHmf <- split(bbgrey, covariates(bbgrey)$sex)
secr.fit(CHmf,...)

messages.subject: Binomial count bug fixed in pre-release 3.1.4
messages.subject_clean: Binomial count bug fixed in pre-release 3.1.4
messages.body_plain: Versions 3.0.1 to 3.1.3 contained a bug that caused secr.fit to fail or produce bad estimates with binomial count data derived by collapsing binary data from multiple occasions -- including with reduce(..., by = 'all', output = 'count'). When secr.fit is called with count data and binomN = 1 the usage at each detector is treated as the 'size' of a binomial probability (the maximum possible number of observations of an animal). However, the C code for this part of the likelihood was corrupted in secr 3.0.1 (May 2017). The problem is fixed in secr 3.1.4, available on the Density website <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/SECRinR.html> in pre-release form. Thanks to Mathias Tobler for reporting the issue.

messages.subject: RE: 95% Home Range from sigma
messages.body_plain:
I followed up with David Ringler on this as its come up a few times on the list now:

We used the circular.r function to determine the sigma multiplier.
Assuming a hazard rate detection function and a z-estimate of 4 (which indeed is not in the paper), that gives :

circular.r(detectfn=1, detectpar=list(sigma=1, z=4), hazard=FALSE)
multiplier = 3.36

Also at the time we did that, integration of the circular.r function was not performed on the cumulative hazard rate. Using that new integration, the multiplier would be :

circular.r(detectfn=1, detectpar=list(sigma=1, z=4), hazard=TRUE)
multiplier = 1.8 (which is changing a bit our HR estimates)

James

From: secr...@googlegroups.com [mailto:secr...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Murray Efford
Sent: Friday, 1 December 2017 5:53 AM
To: secr <secr...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: 95% Home Range from sigma

Hi
Check the help for circular.r in 'secr'. The bivariate-normal multiplier is indeed around 19 (it also depends on whether you believe the hazard or the probability has a bivariate normal distribution). I think one of Beth Gardner's papers is a peer-reviewed source for SECR, and there are many others going back to Calhoun & Casby and Jennrich & Turner. I can't make sense of Ringler et al. They use a hazard-rate detection function for which the multiplier depends strongly on z, yet, as far as I can see on a quick browse, they do not acknowledge this or report their z-hat.

Whatever you do - remember this is really rough and depends on an implausible model for animal behaviour, so agreement with telemetry data is not expected.
Murray

messages.subject: Best Method for clipping non habitat from mask
messages.subject_clean: Best Method for clipping non habitat from mask
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to create a mask that identifies habitat vs. non habitat based on elevation. I have a DEM(elevation) in raster format that I added a column labelled "Habitat" that is binary, ie anything <= 8,500 ft is habitat marked with "1". I have imported this into R and converted it to SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.

I have tried a couple methods:
DEM2 is the SpatialPolygonsDataFrame with the binary Habitat column.

mask.3000<- make.mask(traps, buffer = 3000, type = "trapbuffer")
mask1<-addCovariates(mask.3000, DEM2, columns="Habitat", replace=F)

I get "NAs" for the entire Habitat column. So the mask is unchanged.

I've also tried:
mask.3000<- make.mask(traps, buffer = 3000, type = "trapbuffer", poly = DEM2, keep.poly = TRUE)
This also does not apply any of the habitat information, only the bounding box information.

Is there a better file format to use for the raster conversion?

The resolution of the raster is much higher than the mask grid, does this cause issues if the pixel size is not the same?

I appreciate any and all help,
Colby

messages.body_plain:
Hi Colby
If your DEM is indeed a 'raster' object then David Borcher's offline reply to Ryan Kinderman's recent question may be adapted:
covariates(mask.3000) <- data.frame(Habitat = extract(DEM, mask.3000, spatial=TRUE)) # extract at mask coordinates and put them in the mask covariate named "Habitat"
I don't think this ever made it onto the list as David intended. I've tweaked the original by assuming that because a mask is a sort of (inherits from) data.frame it can be used directly in extract(). If that fails then pre-build a dataframe with columns x,y.
I'm not promising as I don't have rasters on hand to test it, but it may work.
Murray

messages.subject_clean: Best Method for clipping non habitat from mask
messages.body_plain:
As I understand it, pixels with Habitat = 0 don't belong in your mask (no animal could live there). You can drop them with something like
newmask <- subset(mask.3000, covariates(mask.3000)$Habitat > 0)
See also ?subset.mask.

That's it - no need to add anything to the model specification, just provide mask = newmask in secr.fit()

Murray
